protections: Bound the resources spent inflating a JWE 'zip':'DEF' payload after decryption: a limit on the compressed input (A) and a limit on the decompressed output (B). Both apply at the single decompression call, so they are one protection with two parts.

evidence: jwcrypto/jwe.py:425 zlib.decompress(data, -zlib.MAX_WBITS) runs with no size check on data and no max output length
jwcrypto/jwe.py:31-45 module defaults hold only algorithm lists; there is no size limit (compare jwcrypto/jwa.py:31 and jwa.py:593, the only resource limit in the package, for PBES2 p2c)

traps.reason_to_dismiss: Capping len(data) before decompressing (the A-style fix) looks like it fully closes the bomb, but a payload under the cap can still inflate by about 1000x.
evidence: jwcrypto/jwe.py:425 one-shot zlib.decompress with no max_length; a check on compressed length would sit at the same line and would not bound the output

traps.reason_to_dismiss: All recipients go through _decrypt, so a guard placed there already covers every recipient.
evidence: jwcrypto/jwe.py:451-453 decrypt() calls _decrypt for every recipient, so each successful recipient decompresses again
jwcrypto/jwe.py:373 the per-recipient header is merged into jh, which supplies 'zip' at jwe.py:423

traps.reason_to_dismiss: JWT only delegates to JWE.decrypt, so it is the same sink.
evidence: jwcrypto/jwt.py:668 creates JWE() for 5-part tokens; jwt.py:628 validate_fn = self.token.decrypt reaches jwe.py:425

traps.reason_to_dismiss: Where 'zip' comes from does not change how much is inflated, and RFC 7516 placement is an integrity concern, not CWE-409.
evidence: jwcrypto/jwe.py:172-177 'zip' is accepted from the unprotected and per-recipient headers as well as the protected header, then read at jwe.py:423

masking: T2 shows up only after an input-length cap for T1 (the A fix) is in place; before that, T1 already covers the whole bomb.

conflicts.what: A cap that is too low (on compressed or decompressed size) breaks legitimate compressed tokens. jwe.py:199 produces DEF payloads that must still round-trip through jwe.py:425.

fairness_risks: Legitimate zip:'DEF' JWEs (produced at jwcrypto/jwe.py:197-199) must keep decrypting. The hidden tests must use a limit or exception the report states, because the pinned code has no named size constant (jwe.py:31-45) to anchor one.
The tests cannot pin the exception type for an oversized payload: decrypt() catches it and re-raises InvalidJWEData (jwcrypto/jwe.py:459-470).

T5: refusing 'zip' outside the protected header would break callers who put it in unprotected headers today (jwe.py:172-177). No zip tests exist in jwcrypto/tests.py or tests-cookbook.py to show what callers rely on.

design.why: There is a single decompression sink (jwcrypto/jwe.py:425). Every route (multi-recipient, JWT, JWKSet loop) passes through _decrypt, so one bounded-decompressobj fix closes T1-T4. T5 is off-CWE hardening. That leaves at most 2 groups, and no deepseek-type trap (a route with the protection absent and a strong reason to dismiss). The 3-5 trap minimum cannot be met. The only real stacking value is the A-then-B layering (input cap vs output cap) at one line. That works as a single medium/hard M8 trap, not a stack.

unverified: Contents of A fix 90477a3b6e73: from memory, it added default_max_compressed_size (256 KiB) and a len(data) check before zlib.decompress in jwe.py _decrypt. The pinned tree predates it and the commit was not read.
Contents of B fix 25db861d8b29: assumed to bound decompressed output (e.g. zlib.decompressobj with max_length). Not read.
The pinned commit 240cc60 (after Version 1.5.5) predates both fixes, so the task would ask for A+B together. Whether the benchmark intends to pin after A instead was not checked.

That the attacker needs only the recipient's public key (RSA-OAEP/ECDH-ES), so the sink is reachable before any authentication. This follows from the algorithms at jwe.py:37-40 but was not traced through jwa.py.
